title: I Am No Crane (The Teaching of Dharmavyadha)
body:
I Am No Crane (The Teaching of Dharmavyadha)

कर्मण्येवाधिकारस्ते मा फलेषु कदाचन ।
मा कर्मफलहेतुर्भूर्मा ते सङ्गोऽस्त्वकर्मणि ।।

"You have a right to perform your prescribed duties, but you are not entitled to the fruits of your actions. Never consider yourself to be the cause of the results of your activities, nor be attached to inaction. (Gita II-47)"

The sage Markandeya comforted the Pandavas with the story of Kausika, a proud ascetic who had acquired great yogic power through penance. One day, while Kausika was meditating under a tree, a crane defiled his head with its droppings. Kausika looked up in anger, and his burning glance instantly killed the bird. Though pained by his action, Kausika became highly vain about his power.
Later, Kausika went to a town to beg for alms, standing outside a house. The housewife kept him waiting for a long time as she was dutifully serving her sick husband. When she finally approached Kausika, he rebuked her severely for disrespecting a Brahmin. The housewife smiled and said: 'O sage, be not angry. I am no crane to be killed by a violent thought. Your rage can do no harm to a woman who devotes herself to her duty.'
Taken aback, Kausika asked how she knew of the crane incident. She replied: 'Go to Mithila and be instructed in the secret of duty by Dharmavyadha—a humble butcher.' Kausika traveled to Mithila, shocked to find that the wise preceptor was a butcher selling meat in a busy shop. Dharmavyadha taught him that the highest spiritual perfection is attained not by outer asceticism or scriptural pride, but by the sincere, ego-free execution of one's own duty (Swadharma). Kausika returned home to serve his aged parents, transforming his raw learning into true, lived virtue.
